knowledge.answer: Both Christianity and Islam honour Jesus, but they understand Him very differently. Islam teaches that Jesus (Isa) was one of Allah's greatest prophets, born of a virgin, the Messiah sent to Israel and a worker of miracles, but not the Son of God. Muslims deny His divinity, crucifixion and resurrection. Christians believe that Jesus is the eternal Son of God who entered creation as a man, fulfilled Old Testament prophecy, died on the cross for our sins and rose again. Christians also believe Jesus possesses divine authority and offers salvation to all who trust in Him. While Muslims often reject the title 'Son of God' because they understand 'begotten' to imply biological generation, Christians reject this interpretation. In Christian theology, the Son is eternal, uncreated and fully equal with the Father, and 'begotten' describes His unique relationship with the Father rather than a physical origin.

knowledge.answer: Christians believe Jesus revealed His divinity through both His words and His actions. Daniel 7:13-14 describes the divine Son of Man who receives worship and everlasting dominion. When Jesus applied this prophecy to Himself before the Jewish leaders (Matthew 26:64; Mark 14:62), they understood it as a claim to divine authority. Jesus also forgave sins in Mark 2:5-12, prompting the religious leaders to ask, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' Rather than correcting them, Jesus demonstrated His authority to forgive sins. Christians therefore argue that Jesus did not merely claim divinity, He exercised it. This is precisely why the Jewish leaders sought His crucifixion, accusing Him of blasphemy for making Himself equal with God. Interestingly, the Quran acknowledges that Jesus was sentenced to be crucified, but teaches that He was not actually crucified and was instead raised up by Allah. Christians note that similar ideas existed centuries before Islam among some early groups who struggled with the idea of God entering creation and suffering in human flesh. Some taught that Jesus only appeared to have a physical body, while others claimed that His suffering and death only appeared to happen. By contrast, historic Christianity teaches that Jesus is fully God and fully man, truly died on the cross and truly rose again. Christians therefore see the crucifixion not as a contradiction of Jesus' divinity, but as the ultimate demonstration of God's plan of redemption.

knowledge.answer: The Trinity is the Christian belief that God has always existed as three eternal persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who together are one divine being. This did not begin at creation but reflects God's eternal nature. The Son entered creation as Jesus Christ while remaining fully God. Christians believe the Old Testament contains hints of this plurality, including appearances of the Angel of the Lord and concepts such as the Two Powers in Heaven. The New Testament reveals the fullness of God's triune nature, showing the Father drawing people to the Son through the Holy Spirit. Christians do not believe in three gods, but one God in a tri-personal unity. Because God exists outside space and time, aspects of His nature remain mysterious. Many Christians conclude that the Trinity is not forced into Scripture; rather, Scripture itself leads us to it.

knowledge.answer: In Christianity, 'Son of God' does not mean that God physically fathered a child. Christians believe Jesus is the eternal Son who has always existed with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The title describes His unique relationship with the Father and His divine identity. Throughout Scripture, spiritual beings, kings and even Israel are sometimes called 'sons of God', but Jesus stands apart from all of them. He is the unique Son who shares the Father's nature, fulfils God's promises and possesses authority over creation, sin and death. Many Muslims reject the title because they understand 'Son' or 'begotten Son' in a biological sense, but Christians do not. In Christian theology, 'begotten' speaks of Jesus' unique relationship, honour and pre-eminence rather than a physical origin. This is why demons recognise Him as the Son of God, why He exercises divine authority throughout the Gospels, and why Christians believe He is God incarnate rather than merely a prophet.

knowledge.topic: Why Can't Good Works Save Us?
keywords: why can't good works save us
knowledge.answer: Christianity teaches that good works cannot save us because our deepest problem is not a lack of good deeds but a broken relationship with God caused by sin. Jesus illustrates this in the Parable of the Prodigal Son. The younger brother is lost through open rebellion, while the elder brother is lost through pride and self-righteousness. One sins by breaking the rules, the other by trusting in his own obedience. Both are separated from the father and both need grace. The parable shows that neither rebellion nor religion can save us. Salvation comes only through God's mercy, not through our performance. This is why Christians believe Jesus, the true Elder Brother, came to seek the lost, bear the cost of reconciliation and bring us home to the Father.

knowledge.topic: Is Christianity About Religion or Relationship?
knowledge.answer: Christianity is often described as a religion, but at its heart it is about a restored relationship with God through Jesus Christ. Many religions focus primarily on what people must do to reach God, but the gospel teaches that God reached down to us. Prayer, fasting, obedience and good works remain important, but they are not ways of earning God's favour. Rather, they flow from knowing and loving Him. As I studied Christianity after leaving Islam, one of the biggest differences I discovered was that following Christ is not ultimately about performing religious duties but about knowing God personally. Jesus invites the weary to come to Him, promising rest for their souls. Christianity therefore teaches that salvation is not achieved through human effort, but received through God's grace, leading to a relationship that transforms the heart from the inside out.

knowledge.answer: Christians believe that God is sovereign over history and can use even difficult events to accomplish His purposes. Throughout Scripture, God often allowed trials, nations and even periods of judgement to draw His people back to Himself. Some Christians have suggested that the rise of Islam came at a time when much of the visible church had become politically corrupt, divided and spiritually compromised, serving as a historical wake-up call similar to how God disciplined Israel in the Old Testament. While God does not approve of falsehood, He is able to bring good out of human error and rebellion. Historically, the Islamic world helped preserve and transmit important knowledge during Europe's Dark Ages, played a role in developments that contributed to the Age of Discovery, and indirectly created circumstances that allowed the Protestant Reformation to survive and spread. Through these events, the gospel was ultimately carried to many parts of the world that had never previously heard it. We often cannot understand God's purposes in the moment, but in hindsight we frequently see how He uses even painful chapters of history to achieve greater ends. Just as God can use trials in an individual's life for good, Christians trust that He is also working through the rise and fall of nations according to His sovereign plan.

knowledge.answer: The Islamic Dilemma highlights a tension between the Quran and the Bible. The Quran affirms the Torah and Gospel as genuine revelations from God, yet differs from them on major issues such as the identity, divinity and crucifixion of Jesus. If the Bible was preserved, Islam contradicts God's earlier revelation. If the Bible was corrupted, the Quran is mistaken for affirming it. Christians therefore argue that the Quran cannot both confirm and contradict the biblical message.

knowledge.answer: The Sabbath was established by God as a day of rest and worship. In the Old Testament, Israel was commanded to rest on the seventh day as a reminder that God is the Creator who rested after His work of creation and the Redeemer who delivered His people from slavery. However, the Sabbath was never intended to be merely a religious duty or a set of rules. Its deeper purpose was to direct people towards trusting and delighting in God. Jesus taught that 'the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27), correcting those who had turned it into a burden. Christians believe the Sabbath ultimately points to Christ, who offers true rest for weary souls. As Jesus said, 'Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). For this reason, many Christians gather for worship on Sunday, celebrating Christ's resurrection, whilst recognising that our deepest rest is found not in observing a particular day but in knowing Him. The Sabbath reminds us that following God is not primarily about performing religious duties to earn His favour, but about trusting Him, resting in His grace and growing in a relationship with Him.
